top_vulnerabilities.name: CSP: Failure to Define Directive with No Fallback
top_vulnerabilities.description: The Content Security Policy fails to define one of the directives that has no fallback. Missing/excluding them is the same as allowing anything.
top_vulnerabilities.solution: Ensure that your web server, application server, load balancer, etc. is properly configured to set the Content-Security-Policy header.

top_vulnerabilities.name: Content Security Policy (CSP) Header Not Set
top_vulnerabilities.description: Content Security Policy (CSP) is an added layer of security that helps to detect and mitigate certain types of attacks, including Cross Site Scripting (XSS) and data injection attacks. These attacks are used for everything from data theft to site defacement or distribution of malware. CSP provides a set of standard HTTP headers that allow website owners to declare approved sources of content that browsers should be allowed to load on that page — covered types are JavaScript, CSS, HTML frames, fo
top_vulnerabilities.solution: Ensure that your web server, application server, load balancer, etc. is configured to set the Content-Security-Policy header.

top_vulnerabilities.name: Cross-Domain Misconfiguration
top_vulnerabilities.description: Web browser data loading may be possible, due to a Cross Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) misconfiguration on the web server.
top_vulnerabilities.solution: Ensure that sensitive data is not available in an unauthenticated manner (using IP address white-listing, for instance).Configure the "Access-Control-Allow-Origin" HTTP header to a more restrictive set of domains, or remove all CORS headers entirely, to allow the web browser to enforce the Same Origin Policy (SOP) in a more restrictive manner.

top_vulnerabilities.name: Missing Anti-clickjacking Header
top_vulnerabilities.description: The response does not protect against 'ClickJacking' attacks. It should include either Content-Security-Policy with 'frame-ancestors' directive or X-Frame-Options.
top_vulnerabilities.solution: Modern Web browsers support the Content-Security-Policy and X-Frame-Options HTTP headers. Ensure one of them is set on all web pages returned by your site/app.If you expect the page to be framed only by pages on your server (e.g. it's part of a FRAMESET) then you'll want to use SAMEORIGIN, otherwise if you never expect the page to be framed, you should use DENY. Alternatively consider implementing Content Security Policy's "frame-ancestors" directive.

top_vulnerabilities.name: Permissions Policy Header Not Set
top_vulnerabilities.description: Permissions Policy Header is an added layer of security that helps to restrict from unauthorized access or usage of browser/client features by web resources. This policy ensures the user privacy by limiting or specifying the features of the browsers can be used by the web resources. Permissions Policy provides a set of standard HTTP headers that allow website owners to limit which features of browsers can be used by the page such as camera, microphone, location, full screen etc.
top_vulnerabilities.solution: Ensure that your web server, application server, load balancer, etc. is configured to set the Permissions-Policy header.

vulnerabilities.name: Insufficient Site Isolation Against Spectre Vulnerability
vulnerabilities.description: Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header is a response header that prevents a document from loading any cross-origin resources that don't explicitly grant the document permission (using CORP or CORS).
vulnerabilities.solution: Ensure that the application/web server sets the Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header appropriately, and that it sets the Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header to 'require-corp' for documents.If possible, ensure that the end user uses a standards-compliant and modern web browser that supports the Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header (https://caniuse.com/mdn-http_headers_cross-origin-embedder-policy).

Permissions Policy provides a set of standard HTTP headers that allow website owners to limit which features of browsers can be used by the page such as camera, microphone, location, full screen etc.
vulnerabilities.solution: Ensure that your web server, application server, load balancer, etc. is configured to set the Permissions-Policy header.

vulnerabilities.name: Server Leaks Information via "X-Powered-By" HTTP Response Header Field(s)
vulnerabilities.description: The web/application server is leaking information via one or more "X-Powered-By" HTTP response headers. Access to such information may facilitate attackers identifying other frameworks/components your web application is reliant upon and the vulnerabilities such components may be subject to.
vulnerabilities.solution: Ensure that your web server, application server, load balancer, etc. is configured to suppress "X-Powered-By" headers.

vulnerabilities.name: Server Leaks Version Information via "Server" HTTP Response Header Field
vulnerabilities.description: The web/application server is leaking version information via the "Server" HTTP response header. Access to such information may facilitate attackers identifying other vulnerabilities your web/application server is subject to.
vulnerabilities.solution: Ensure that your web server, application server, load balancer, etc. is configured to suppress the "Server" header or provide generic details.

vulnerabilities.name: Strict-Transport-Security Header Not Set
vulnerabilities.description: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) is a web security policy mechanism whereby a web server declares that complying user agents (such as a web browser) are to interact with it using only secure HTTPS connections (i.e. HTTP layered over TLS/SSL). HSTS is an IETF standards track protocol and is specified in RFC 6797.
vulnerabilities.solution: Ensure that your web server, application server, load balancer, etc. is configured to enforce Strict-Transport-Security.

vulnerabilities.name: Timestamp Disclosure - Unix
vulnerabilities.description: A timestamp was disclosed by the application/web server. - Unix
vulnerabilities.solution: Manually confirm that the timestamp data is not sensitive, and that the data cannot be aggregated to disclose exploitable patterns.

vulnerabilities.name: X-Content-Type-Options Header Missing
vulnerabilities.description: The Anti-MIME-Sniffing header X-Content-Type-Options was not set to 'nosniff'. This allows older versions of Internet Explorer and Chrome to perform MIME-sniffing on the response body, potentially causing the response body to be interpreted and displayed as a content type other than the declared content type. Current (early 2014) and legacy versions of Firefox will use the declared content type (if one is set), rather than performing MIME-sniffing.
vulnerabilities.solution: Ensure that the application/web server sets the Content-Type header appropriately, and that it sets the X-Content-Type-Options header to 'nosniff' for all web pages.If possible, ensure that the end user uses a standards-compliant and modern web browser that does not perform MIME-sniffing at all, or that can be directed by the web application/web server to not perform MIME-sniffing.

vulnerabilities.name: Base64 Disclosure
vulnerabilities.description: Base64 encoded data was disclosed by the application/web server. Note: in the interests of performance not all base64 strings in the response were analyzed individually, the entire response should be looked at by the analyst/security team/developer(s).
vulnerabilities.solution: Manually confirm that the Base64 data does not leak sensitive information, and that the data cannot be aggregated/used to exploit other vulnerabilities.

vulnerabilities.name: Information Disclosure - Suspicious Comments
vulnerabilities.description: The response appears to contain suspicious comments which may help an attacker.
vulnerabilities.solution: Remove all comments that return information that may help an attacker and fix any underlying problems they refer to.

vulnerabilities.name: Modern Web Application
vulnerabilities.description: The application appears to be a modern web application. If you need to explore it automatically then the Ajax Spider may well be more effective than the standard one.
vulnerabilities.solution: This is an informational alert and so no changes are required.

vulnerabilities.name: Re-examine Cache-control Directives
vulnerabilities.description: The cache-control header has not been set properly or is missing, allowing the browser and proxies to cache content. For static assets like css, js, or image files this might be intended, however, the resources should be reviewed to ensure that no sensitive content will be cached.
vulnerabilities.solution: For secure content, ensure the cache-control HTTP header is set with "no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate". If an asset should be cached consider setting the directives "public, max-age, immutable".

vulnerabilities.name: Sec-Fetch-Dest Header is Missing
vulnerabilities.description: Specifies how and where the data would be used. For instance, if the value is audio, then the requested resource must be audio data and not any other type of resource.
vulnerabilities.solution: Ensure that Sec-Fetch-Dest header is included in request headers.

vulnerabilities.name: Sec-Fetch-Mode Header is Missing
vulnerabilities.description: Allows to differentiate between requests for navigating between HTML pages and requests for loading resources like images, audio etc.
vulnerabilities.solution: Ensure that Sec-Fetch-Mode header is included in request headers.

vulnerabilities.name: Sec-Fetch-Site Header is Missing
vulnerabilities.description: Specifies the relationship between request initiator's origin and target's origin.
vulnerabilities.solution: Ensure that Sec-Fetch-Site header is included in request headers.

vulnerabilities.name: Sec-Fetch-User Header is Missing
vulnerabilities.description: Specifies if a navigation request was initiated by a user.
vulnerabilities.solution: Ensure that Sec-Fetch-User header is included in user initiated requests.

vulnerabilities.name: Storable and Cacheable Content
vulnerabilities.description: The response contents are storable by caching components such as proxy servers, and may be retrieved directly from the cache, rather than from the origin server by the caching servers, in response to similar requests from other users. If the response data is sensitive, personal or user-specific, this may result in sensitive information being leaked. In some cases, this may even result in a user gaining complete control of the session of another user, depending on the configuration of the caching
vulnerabilities.solution: Validate that the response does not contain sensitive, personal or user-specific information. If it does, consider the use of the following HTTP response headers, to limit, or prevent the content being stored and retrieved from the cache by another user:Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, privatePragma: no-cacheExpires: 0This configuration directs both HTTP 1.0 and HTTP 1.1 compliant caching servers to not store the response, and to not retrieve the response (without validation)
